This could be badly misunderstood, so the safeguards need to be explicit. The adults still have to pay attention to what goes on in a children's territory. Older kids can't be allowed to quietly lord it over the younger ones there, and secrecy can't pass for independence.

I also reject the suburban panic that treats any warm relationship between a child and an unrelated adult as suspicious. It's good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something's wrong. Fear like that can destroy that gift without actually preventing abuse.
community-s8j/u1.A:
This isn't meant to be taken the wrong way and there are definite safegaurds that need to be in place. Adults still need to be aware of what is going on in the territory of the kids. Older kids can't be lordng it over the young kids in the territory, secrecy, etc.

And I am not talking about the fear that seems to pervade so much of suburban America that if a kid is close to any adult that isn't related to them, they must be getting molested. Kids need a bunch of adults in their life that like them and that will take action if need be.
community-s8j/u1.B:
With the understanding that this could be misconstrued I would add that the adults still need to be watchful of what goes on in the kid's territory. Older kids need to be prevented from lordign it over in the kid's territory and things can't be kept secret there.

And I don't mean the sometimes overzealous suburban fear of kids having any relationship with any adult who is not related to them. It is good for kids to have a bunch of adults who are interested in them and who would notice and act on any bad goings-on.

community-s8j/u2.input:
There are several parts to this protection:

Give children real agency. Their "no" matters, and no grownup has a right to their affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.

Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it's about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. A surprise has an end date. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren't allowed.
community-s8j/u2.A:
There are a few parts to this.

One is empowering kids to know that they can say NO, and that no grownup has the right to their love, physical contact, obedience (outside of legitimate safety needs), or access to them.

The other is to set a rule that no grownup has the right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or other trusted adult. It could be about a gift, a game they play together, physical contact, a conversation, a relationship, whatever – no grownup is allowed to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom. A surprise is different, because it eventually comes to an end, but no secret that serves to isolate the kid is allowed.
community-s8j/u2.B:
There are a few parts to this.

1. Children have agency, and the ability to say no. No grownup should ever have the right to a kid’s affection, physical contact, obedience (outside of legitimate safety needs), or access.

2. No secrets. No grownup has the right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or other trusted adult. This applies to any secrets – about gifts, playing, touching, talking, getting to know each other, or any sort of relationship. A surprise is different because it will eventually be revealed, but other types of secrets that have the potential to isolate a kid should not be allowed.

Don't let the teaching turn into interrogation, punishment when they're not sure, or a reason to brush off what they report. A scared or confused kid may not tell the story perfectly and still need protection.

community-s8j/u4.input: Kids also need transferable skills and education, relationships with people outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, or another community). If the community can also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, help with travel, tools or a little money, great. But even if it can't, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving, or holding back the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function outside the community. No upbringing provides perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8j/u4.A: Things to consider for kids: Do they get some education and skills that are valuable outside the community? Do they have any relationships with people outside the community? Does the community give them their records and documents when they leave? Do they have any options for what to do next (school, apprentice, job, family, new community, etc)? Does the community help them with resources to make a smooth transition? Failing that, does the community not make leaving worse, by holding back their records and education? Nothing can give someone total freedom to choose their life, there's always some path dependence, but there are some things a community can do.
community-s8j/u4.B:
Here's some things the community can do (that aren't too hard) to make it easier for the kids to leave if they want to: 1) give them a decent level of education and experience in transferable skills 2) allow them to form relationships with people outside the community 3) allow them to have/see/access their own records and documents 4) make sure they have at least one obvious choice of where to go (school, apprenticeship, job, family, other community, etc.) 5) if possible, give them some resources to make the transition easier if not, at least avoid actively punishing them for leaving or withholding information/records/etc.

No, this doesn't give them perfect freedom of choice and doesn't eliminate path dependency, but it's a start.

community-s8j/u5.input:
Couples who live together, share the same culture and even the same bed still split over screens, vaccinations, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. And that's just two people. Now think of twenty adults, all with different childhoods.

Once a kid is already living inside the disagreement, goodwill doesn't answer those questions. The community has to share enough principles about raising kids to offer them coherence, and leave parents enough room to remain parents.
community-s8j/u5.A:
Even couples that sleep in the same bed, come from the same culture and live together disagree on how to raise their kids. It can be over screen time, or vaccinations, or schooling, or religion, or what they eat, or how they are disciplined, or how their medical needs are met. And this is between two people!

When there are twenty adults involved, and the kids are already in the mix, how can such differences be overcome? In order for this to work, it is essential that the adults in the community share some principles about raising kids. These principles need to be general enough to allow parents to be parents, but specific enough to create coherence in the community.
community-s8j/u5.B:
Couples living in the same culture, in the same bed, disagree on screens and vaccinations and school and religion and food and kid-discipline and medical care. This is just between two people, with very different childhoods.

When kids are on the scene, good will isn’t enough to resolve disagreements. The communities into which the kids are born need to share some guiding principles about how kids are raised, and to strike a balance between communal coherence and parental freedom.

community-s8j/u6.input:
I mention vaccination specifically because it's one of the values I would absolutely need to share with people in a community, if I was going to raise children there. I'm not trying to design a village for everyone, only saying that communities need some common ground among the parents on children's health, enough that they can actually trust one another.

All of this will ultimately be reviewed by the kids, once they're grown, and their review weighs more heavily than founders usually want it to. Adults can go on about their intentions forever, but the kids who lived through it might have something else to say.
community-s8j/u6.A:
*I used the example of vaccination above, but this could be anything that is important to me as a parent. I’m not laying out the requisite values for all people in a new intentional village, I’m just saying that in order to create a community that I would want my kids to be a part of, there would need to be a significant concensus amongst the parents about a certain set of issues relating to the health of the children.

Keep in mind that this will be reviewed by the kids later, and their review will be weighty, even if the founders don’t want it to be.
community-s8j/u6.B:
Actually I'm glad it's vaccination, something that if I had to bring up children in a community, would be something I absolutely had to find common ground on. While I'm not designing a village for all, I do think that it's important for all the parents in a village to have a reasonable common ground on children's health, so that they can trust each other.

Oh yeah, they will review their experience, and it will be weighted heavily. Not that the adult founders want to hear what the kids have to say!
